rv.q: My favorite comes near the end, after a mass migration to the other side , when a few lingering souls not ready to cross over wake up and discover that they “had again been granted the great mother-gift: time. More time.” What is opera if not a granting of that gift?

Lincoln (Peter Mattei), the opera’s only living character, visits the graveyard alone at night, mourning his child. The principal ghost narrators—Vollman (Ryan McKinny), Bevins (Jonah Hoskins) and the Reverend (Christine Goerke)—are determined to get Willie to move on to the next phase of existence, since the bardo is a bad place for children.
The bravura aria that Mazzoli gives her at the start of the second act—soaring and droll, and slowly intensifying—is a musical delight.

Happily, the composer Missy Mazzoli and the librettist Royce Vavrek, both riding high off the acclaimed premiere of The Galloping Cure at the Edinburgh International Festival, ensured this operatic adaptation ascended to spectacular heights.
As portrayed in Lileana Blain-Cruz's blazing production, it is a place of wonder.
It’s a thrilling overture to a mostly disappointing night.
For all its preoccupation with death, this is an opera that lives.
An astonishing piece of theater, Lincoln in the Bardo beautifully unearths the message that ultimate healing comes from willingly engaging in ultimate empathy.
Solid story structure, a brilliant production, and, above all, a glorious score imbued with life by a fantastic cast make this a must-see showcase at the Met.
Under Yannick Nézet-Séguin’s ever-attentive baton, the Met Orchestra sounded energetic and polished throughout the night, as they navigated Mazzoli’s mercurial and blazingly colorful score.
The anticipation paid off: words, music and stagecraft fused into a remarkably cohesive whole, creating a theatrical experience of rare power.
Lincoln largely avoided becoming bogged down in American mythologizing, offering instead a lushly scored and beautifully sung little slice of death.
Intriguing, at times moving, at other times frustrating, Lincoln in the Bardo is perhaps the appropriate expression of a post-mortal world of inner confusion and mystery.

cn.t: Mazzoli's historic Met commission earns mostly strong reviews for its moving, atmospheric adaptation of Saunders' novel, with critics praising its emotional impact and immersive staging, though some find the opera disappointing despite its ambitious literary source.
